title: Dawnshade - Why it isn't for me
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aQF7qqm1iHE

A week after the unboxing, Daniel (@dungeondive) explains why Dawnshade is going on the sell pile — carefully framed as not a review, since he hasn't played enough to call it one, only enough to know it isn't for him.

The praise is real: outstanding production, thick cardboard, good art, writing better than most narrative board games manage. He likes the adventure board, the stack of quest tiles built fresh each game, the threat track that ends a scenario once you've moved enough spaces, and the fact that a whole campaign runs only three games — manageable, finishable.

The problem is the join between the two halves. Nearly every non-combat challenge resolves through a dexterity mini-game: rolling dice shuffleboard-style at a target band, a lock-picking game rolling a token between stacked chips without toppling them, gambling flips, sliding, even a two-player spinning-top duel. His objection is precise — the game sells deep character builds, but almost nothing you do to a challenge depends on how you built your character. It depends on how good you are at flicking things.

His verdict is that this should have been sold as a themed dexterity game, leaned into fully, which would have made it genuinely unique. Instead it sits in a middle ground he can't identify an audience for. The elemental balance board, meanwhile, he found himself ignoring.

----

Should a game be judged against what it is, or against what its marketing led you to expect?
